Field surveys conducted across the tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific have established that the Striped bonito, Sarda orientalis, achieves a maximum total length of 102 cm [Li = 102 cm] in large mature individuals, a dimension that situates it as a formidable mid-tier predator within pelagic food webs. Gonadal examination of specimens collected throughout the reproductive season reveals that pubertal transition, marked by the commencement of active gametogenesis, is attained at a considerably smaller body size. The length at which the majority of individuals show evidence of first spawning readiness is approximately 47.8 cm [Lp = approximately 47.8 cm], a value derived from histological staging of ovarian and testicular tissues. This discrepancy between asymptotic size and size at sexual maturation underscores a life-history strategy wherein substantial somatic growth continues well after the onset of reproductive competence, a pattern repeatedly documented among fast-swimming, high-metabolic-rate scombrids that must rapidly attain a size refuge from gape-limited predators before diverting resources toward gonadal investment.

Reproductive events in Sarda orientalis yield pelagic eggs whose dimensions, while not directly measured in the wild, are inferred from congeneric data to approximate those of Sarda chiliensis, with an estimated egg diameter near 1.05 millimeters. Based on the volumetric relationship of a sphere, the wet weight at birth of the emergent yolk-sac larva is calculated to be roughly 0.0006 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0006 grams], a minute initial mass characteristic of teleosts that produce large numbers of small, buoyant ova. The developmental trajectory from fertilisation to hatching is strongly temperature-dependent. Under controlled experimental conditions at a constant 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], which approximates the sea-surface temperatures of core spawning habitats, the incubation period lasts precisely 5 days [ab = precisely 5 days], after which the prolarva ruptures the chorion and enters the plankton as a lecithotrophic, mouth-closed alevin. This rapid embryogenesis facilitates population replenishment in ephemeral upwelling zones where food availability for early larvae is temporally constrained. This diminutive hatchling mass, only six ten-thousandths of a gram, is among the smallest recorded for the tribe Sardini, reflecting the selective advantage of producing enormous numbers of offspring with minimal initial investment per individual larva.

Growth in body mass following the onset of exogenous feeding is rapid. Reared individuals and wild-caught specimens measured across multiple year classes reveal that Striped bonito approach an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 13,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 13,400 grams] in the oldest and largest adults, a mass that places them within the intermediate range among the tribe Sardini. In contrast, the wet weight at which sexual maturation is first recorded, the mass at puberty, is substantially less. Fish sampled at the initial stage of vitellogenesis or active spermiation exhibit a mean body mass of about 1,330 grams [Wwp = about 1,330 grams], indicating that gonadal activation occurs well before somatic growth has ceased. The resulting gap between pubertal and ultimate mass, which spans nearly an order of magnitude, reflects a prolonged growth trajectory that continues long after the first reproductive event. This pattern is consistent with the life-history strategy of iteroparous pelagic predators that face high adult mortality and depend on repeated spawning across multiple seasons to offset variable recruitment success.

Estimates of maximum reproductive output for Sarda orientalis have been obtained from captive spawning trials and from gonad mass–fecundity regressions of wild fish. At a water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], which is maintained during the peak spawning season in equatorial waters, a single spawning event can release up to 446,530 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = up to 446,530 eggs per spawning event]. Reproductive periodicity, inferred from oocyte size-frequency distributions and the seasonal appearance of postovulatory follicles, indicates that females engage in one primary spawning bout each year [F_R_i = one primary spawning bout each year]. The aggregate annual fecundity thus reaches nearly half a million ova, a reproductive capacity that surpasses that of many co-occurring scombrids of similar body mass. Such prodigious egg production is thought to compensate for high egg and larval mortality rates in the warm, predator-dense surface layers, and it aligns with the opportunistic reproductive strategy expected of a fast-growing, short-lived pelagic teleost that exploits transient oceanographic features for larval advection. Such elevated fecundity, when adjusted for body mass, ranks among the highest within the Scombridae, illustrating the species' adaptation to oligotrophic equatorial waters where larval survival probabilities are exceedingly low.

Longevity in Sarda orientalis has been investigated through otolith increment analysis and tag-recapture programs in the western Pacific. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of its tropical range, where ambient temperatures hover near 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], the maximum documented lifespan approaches approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days], which corresponds to a chronological age of about five years [am = about five years]. This relatively abbreviated natural lifespan, when compared to the larger tunas of the genus Thunnus, reflects a fast life-history pace: early maturation, elevated metabolic rates sustained by continuous swimming, and substantial investment in reproductive output all contribute to physiological senescence that curtails longevity. The combination of a five-year maximum age and high annual fecundity underscores a demographic reliance on rapid population turnover rather than individual persistence, a feature that renders Striped bonito populations sensitive to recruitment fluctuations driven by climate-mediated shifts in larval survival. The observed lifespan aligns with the expected longevity for a scombrid of this size, and the age structure derived from otolith-based catch curves indicates a mortality schedule that essentially completes turnover within six years under natural conditions, a demographic pattern typical of short-lived pelagic forage species.
